Preprint — arXiv:2602.00180v1, labelled 'Technical Report'; no published venue
Not stated (single author, location only: Seattle, USA)
Conceptual — practitioner's guide: specification spectrum, generic SDD workflow, tool survey, three illustrative case studies, decision framework. No empirical evaluation

Generic SDD workflow (Specify, Plan, Implement, Validate), no version. Tools surveyed descriptively, no versions: GitHub Spec Kit, Amazon Kiro, Tessl (AI-assisted SDD); also BDD (Cucumber, SpecFlow, Behave), TDD frameworks, API specs (OpenAPI, GraphQL SDL, Protocol Buffers/gRPC, AsyncAPI), contract testing (Pact, Specmatic), model-based design (Simulink, SCADE)

Functional specification (user stories, Given/When/Then scenarios or input-output examples, business rules, edge cases, acceptance criteria); technical plan (architecture, data models, interfaces, technology choices, non-functional requirements); discrete reviewable tasks; unit/acceptance tests encoding spec requirements. Spec Kit described as /specify, /plan, /tasks, implement; Kiro as requirements, design, tasks

Specify (what to build) -> Plan (how to build) -> Implement (tasks, small validated increments) -> Validate (automated tests, BDD scenarios, stakeholder acceptance), with a loop back to refine the spec if validation reveals gaps (Fig. 2)

Human review after Specify, Plan and Implement; Validate is 'Automated + Human' (Fig. 2). Also review/refinement of an LLM-authored ('self-spec') spec before implementation; for Spec Kit, humans review and refine at each phase
Not run, document-based (conceptual description; case studies are illustrative narratives, not executed by the author)

Uses and defines Böckeler-style levels: spec-first, spec-anchored, spec-as-source (Fig. 1); recommends spec-first for AI-assisted initial development, spec-anchored for long-lived production systems ('sweet spot'), spec-as-source only when generation tooling is mature (Tessl, Simulink). Limitations of SDD discussed: LLM non-determinism; over-specification, specification rot, spec as bureaucracy, tooling complexity, false confidence (passing spec test does not guarantee correct software); SDD overkill for throwaway prototypes, solo short-lived projects, exploratory coding, simple CRUD; spec-as-source practical only where generation trust is established
